source.title: Inference-Time Concept Suppression and Video-Centric Evaluation for Text-to-Video Models

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether jailbreak-style prompting recovers a suppressed visual concept, extending the question to text-to-video generators and video-level outcomes rather than LLM knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper tests jailbreak robustness only for nudity, using paraphrase, role-play, obfuscation, and safety-bypass prompts. It reports jailbreak failure and frame-hit rates. It does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or recovery through prompting without an unlearning intervention. The other forgetting, preservation, and quality results are not rows here because they do not measure recovery under an attack.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (text-to-video diffusion generators rather than LLMs), the study measures whether jailbreak prompts bring back a suppressed concept (nudity) for five suppression methods. The results bear on E (prompting recovers) and on F (SIRUS presented as more robust). This is a different kind of system, so it transfers to the LLM-knowledge claim only by analogy.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say SIRUS gives the best preservation-aware jailbreak robustness among methods that don't collapse the subject (24.0% failure, 21.9% frame hit). VideoEraser and Refusal Vector stay highly vulnerable to recovery under adversarial prompts. SAFREE's and T2VUnlearning's lower rates come with severe subject collapse and should be read cautiously.
record.recipe_differences: SIRUS is a training-free, inference-time concept-suppression method for text-to-video diffusion models; it is not one of the listed LLM unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported robustness evaluation is limited to nudity and a jailbreak prompt set containing paraphrase, indirect description, role-play, obfuscation, and safety-bypass phrasing.
record.problems: The jailbreak study is restricted to nudity; no sample counts, uncertainty estimates, or unlearned-model jailbreak baseline are stated. SAFREE and T2VUnlearning have very low person retention under attack, complicating interpretation of their low failure rates.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows: the paper's remaining reported results concern ordinary forgetting, preservation, video quality, or efficiency rather than recovery under prompting attacks.

untested.parts: No LLM, no targeted-knowledge accuracy versus chance. Standard forgetting is measured only as video concept detection.
No activation-direction ablation and no blocked-versus-deleted analysis.

Only nudity, only jailbreak prompts adapted from T2VSafetyBench, only on CogVideoX/OpenSora2. No other-language or in-context attacks. No jailbreak test on Wan2.2 or on church, truck, parachute or Van Gogh.
SIRUS's resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization or adaptive attacks is not tested. Only nudity jailbreaks are tested.

missing.what: Standard-prompt nudity failure and frame-hit rates per method, needed as the baseline for the jailbreak rows; currently 'not stated' in the rows.

Person retention, CSDR and CLIP ratio under jailbreak attack (SIRUS 72.9%, VideoEraser 79.7%, Refusal Vector 81.4%, SAFREE 25.7%, T2VUnlearning 9.5% person retention). These are needed to judge whether low jailbreak rates reflect collapse.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is text-to-video concept suppression, not LLM knowledge unlearning. SIRUS, VideoEraser and SAFREE are inference-time sampling interventions; T2VUnlearning and Refusal Vector modify weights. SIRUS is the authors' own method, so the F evidence is self-reported. No sample counts or uncertainty are given; the 2-point rate granularity suggests about 50 prompts per condition. Refusal Vector is on a different backbone (OpenSora2). The reader's labels marking Refusal Vector as supporting E are unsound: it never forgot the concept on standard prompts.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure targeted-knowledge accuracy relative to chance in an LLM or establish that attacks fail to recover it.
No fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing whether the concept is blocked rather than deleted.
Tests jailbreak-style prompt attacks on nudity only; does not test other languages, in-context information, or non-jailbreak prompt rephrasing separately.
Tests SIRUS against the evaluated nudity jailbreak prompts only; does not test resistance to fine-tuning, internal edits, or quantization.

relation.reason: Measures whether jailbreak prompts recover the suppressed nudity concept, for five suppression methods.

tranche.reason: New setting (text-to-video diffusion concept suppression), with jailbreak-recovery results for five methods.

source_check.notes: Baselines come from Table 1/7 on standard UnlearnDiffAtk-adapted prompts; jailbreak values come from Table 10 on T2VSafetyBench-adapted prompts, so the sets are not paired. Failure is 100 minus success. No n or uncertainty is given. SIRUS is the authors' own method. Refusal Vector runs on OpenSora2, and its jailbreak rates are below its standard-prompt rates. The r1/r2 state (partial) is read against E.

statements.correction: VideoEraser on CogVideoX (text-to-video), nudity, jailbreak prompts adapted from T2VSafetyBench (paraphrase, role-play, obfuscation, safety-bypass): failure 48.0% to 78.0%, frame hit 39.4% to 74.4% (Tables 7, 10). The standard and jailbreak prompt sets differ.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers or claim for this study. It is cited for r3 and r4, which are text-to-video CogVideoX results from jailbreak prompts adapted from T2VSafetyBench. Those are not SD v1.4 image erasure and not optimized adversarial prompts, so the stated conditions exclude the study. The direction (a conventional eraser regenerates under prompt attack) does fit.

statements.correction: SIRUS (authors' training-free inference-time method), CogVideoX, nudity jailbreak prompts: failure 24.0% (20.0% on standard prompts), frame hit 21.9% (15.9%). VideoEraser: failure 78.0% (48.0%), frame hit 74.4% (39.4%). Text-to-video; jailbreak prompts adapted from T2VSafetyBench.
statements.problem: The study is not described. Its own-method result (SIRUS, r1 and r2) does show little prompt recovery, but r3 and r4 (VideoEraser, not the authors' method) show large recovery and don't belong under against. The conditions omit text-to-video. The record's verdict for SIRUS on E is limits_scope (small nonzero rise), not challenges.

statements.correction: SIRUS on CogVideoX, nudity: jailbreak failure 24.0% (20.0% standard), frame hit 21.9% (15.9% standard). VideoEraser (CogVideoX) rises from 48.0% to 78.0% failure and from 39.4% to 74.4% frame hit. Refusal Vector (OpenSora2) scores 66.0%/59.0% under jailbreak, against 72.0%/65.5% on standard prompts (weak suppression throughout).
statements.problem: Makes no claim about this study, which is cited for r1 and r2. SIRUS does largely resist jailbreak prompts, but in text-to-video on CogVideoX, not SD v1.4 erasure. Only nudity was tested, so concept dependence isn't shown here. The rise is small but nonzero (the record's E verdict is limits_scope).

statements.correction: SIRUS on CogVideoX, nudity jailbreak prompts: failure 20.0% to 24.0%, frame hit 15.9% to 21.9%. Authors: strongest preservation-aware robustness among methods that do not collapse the subject. Text-to-video.
statements.problem: Says robust methods are breached by prompt attacks, but r1 and r2 show SIRUS largely resisting jailbreak prompts (+4 points failure, +6 points frame hit). That is not a breach, so challenges is wrong for this study. The setting is text-to-video, not SD v1.4.
